Best road bike mudguards 2026 reviewed

The best road bike mudguards will protect you from road spray and not make a lot of noise in the process. Fitting mudguards to your road bike is a surefire way to stay dry, comfy and infinitely more presentable, plus they’ll also protect your bike’s components from wear, and even keep riders behind you from getting a face full of road grime.

Whether you prefer to have mudguards fitted all year round, or only opt for them in winter when the weather turns, they’re without a doubt one of the best upgrades you can make to your bike. There are also a lot of different types on offer, from full-length fenders secured permanently with metal stays, to plastic clip-ons that you can put on and take off as and when you need them. There are also gravel bike mudguards available that handle the extra width of gravel bike tyres.

To help you decide which type of mudguard is best for your road bike, we’ve rounded up our favourites below. And if you still need some more guidance, keep scrolling for our guide on the different mudguard styles and what’s needed to fit them.

Why you can trust Cyclist’s advice

As riders ourselves, we’re always out reviewing and testing bikes, whatever the weather. So when it comes to the essential task of keeping comfortable on cold, wet rides, we’ll even resort to adding mudguards to an aero bike.

Just take a look at former Cyclist writer Charlotte’s Aeroad Custom Build, shown above, decked out with SKS Raceblades to keep her ride mates happier.

The best road bike mudguards reviewed

Portland Design Works Full Metal Fenders

£119.99 | Buy here

  • Among the quietest metal mudguards we’ve tested
  • Excellent spray protection, with pre-installed rubber mud flaps
  • Straightforward fitting, with adjustable stays

The Portland Design Works Full Metal Fenders are a premium aluminium option that combine generous coverage with impressively quiet running. Thoughtful details include pre-installed rubber mud flaps that extend close to the ground, helping keep both you and anyone riding behind you clear of road spray.

They’re also easier to fit than many traditional metal mudguards. Adjustable stays minimise the need for cutting, while anti-rattle stickers help keep unwanted noise to a minimum. The instructions could be clearer, but fitting is manageable at home without extensive mechanical experience.

PDW rates them for tyres up to 30mm, although clearance is on the tighter side with 28mm tyres. They’re best suited to 25-28mm widths, where they offer an excellent combination of coverage, durability and everyday usability.

At £119.99, they’re certainly not cheap, but if you’re after well-designed metal mudguards that are quiet, robust and relatively painless to live with, they’re a strong contender.

Velo Orange Hammered 45mm mudguards 

£75 | Buy here

  • Beautiful hammered aluminium finish
  • Excellent full-length coverage for tyres up to 35mm
  • Solid, durable construction for long-term use

If aesthetics matter as much as practicality, the Velo Orange Hammered 45mm mudguards are a particularly handsome option. Their distinctive hammered aluminium finish gives them a lovely vintage look, making them especially well suited to steel touring, gravel and hybrid bikes.

They’re also impressively robust, with solid metal fittings and generous full-length coverage that does an excellent job of keeping road spray at bay. The 45mm profile accommodates tyres up to 35mm, making them a good choice for riders running wider rubber.

However, fitting is a fairly involved process. There’s plenty of fiddly hardware to assemble, the stays need cutting to length, and you’ll ideally want a workstand, hacksaw and a few workshop tools to get everything sitting properly. The supplied mounting hardware is also a little limited, so you may need additional bolts or spacers depending on your frame.

Once installed, though, they’re a sturdy, fit-and-forget option that should last for years. They’re not for anyone looking for a quick seasonal installation, but if you’re happy to put in the effort, the combination of excellent coverage, durability and classic looks makes them well worth considering.

SKS Chromoplastic

£49.99 | Buy here

  • Excellent full-length coverage and a neat, close-fitting profile
  • Plenty of adjustment options and widely available spare parts
  • Front safety quick-release helps prevent wheel lock-up

The SKS Chromoplastic P35s are a classic full-length mudguard option, combining a sturdy aluminium core with a plastic outer layer for a durable, practical design. They offer excellent protection against road spray and grime, while a generous selection of supplied bolts and spacers makes it easy to fine-tune their position for a neat fit around your wheels.

A particularly useful feature is the front safety quick-release, which allows the stays to detach if debris becomes trapped between the tyre and mudguard, helping to prevent the front wheel from locking up. They’re also widely stocked, so replacement stays, brackets and other spare parts are readily available.

Fitting is relatively straightforward, although you’ll need to cut the stainless steel stays to length and have a few basic tools to hand. More importantly, check your actual tyre width before buying. Although rated for tyres up to 28mm, real-world measurements can be wider, particularly on wider rims, and clearance is noticeably tighter than on some alternatives. The plastic seatstay bracket is also worth considering if you’re running traditional calliper brakes, as compression can affect brake alignment.

If your tyres fit comfortably within the available clearance, these are a reliable, well-made option for commuting and winter road riding, with excellent coverage and the reassurance of readily available replacement parts.

SKS Raceblade Pro XL

£54.99 | Buy here

  • Extremely quick and easy to fit, with no mudguard mounts needed
  • Fully adjustable to suit different frame and brake setups
  • Easy to remove and transfer between compatible bikes

The SKS Raceblade Pro XLs are a convenient clip-on option for road bikes without traditional mudguard mounts, or for those who don’t want to commit to a permanent winter setup. Secured directly to the fork and seatstays using flexible rubber straps, they’re incredibly quick to install, taking as little as 30 seconds, with no specialist tools required.

Adjustable stays make it easy to position the mudguards around different frame shapes and brake setups, while supplied frame protectors help prevent damage to your paintwork. They’re also easy to remove and refit, making them particularly useful if you only want mudguards when the weather turns.

The compromise is coverage. Although they do a reasonable job of keeping spray off your back and protecting the frame, the short rear guard offers little protection for anyone riding behind you, while the front leaves some spray reaching your hands and face. They’re also prone to rattling on rough roads, thanks to their relatively minimal fixing points.

For solo riding in wet weather, they’re a practical and fuss-free solution. However, if you regularly ride in a group or want proper all-round protection for winter training, a full-length set would be a better choice.

Kinesis Fend Off

£60 | Buy here

  • Robust aluminium and steel construction
  • Quiet running with excellent spray protection
  • Recyclable packaging doubles up as front and rear mud flaps

The Kinesis Fend Offs are a sturdy set of aluminium mudguards that offer excellent coverage and impressively quiet running. Their squared-off profile gives them a distinctive look, while the solid aluminium and steel construction feels reassuringly durable. They’re available in two widths, with the 40mm Standard version accommodating tyres up to 34mm and the 50mm Wide version taking tyres up to 45mm.

They’re relatively straightforward to install for traditional full-length metal mudguards, although you’ll need to cut the stays to length and have a few basic tools to hand. Once fitted, they’re impressively stable, with minimal rattling even over rough roads. A particularly neat touch is the recyclable, low-plastic packaging, which can be repurposed into additional front and rear mud flaps for improved spray protection.

There are a few compromises. Unlike some competitors, they don’t have a front safety quick-release mechanism, and clearance around calliper brakes can be tight. They’re also heavier than plastic alternatives, so aren’t the best choice if keeping weight down is a priority.

However, if you’re after a durable, fit-and-forget set of metal mudguards for year-round riding, the Fend Offs offer an excellent combination of coverage, quiet running and robust construction.

Crud Roadracer Mk3

£49.99 | Buy here

  • Excellent rear coverage, including protection for the drivetrain
  • Quiet running, even with tight tyre clearances
  • Adaptable design for bikes without mudguard mounts

The Crud Catcher Road Racer Mk3 mudguards offer an interesting solution for road bikes that lack traditional mudguard mounts or have limited clearance for conventional full-length mudguards. Their clever plastic design uses adhesive mounting points and adjustable sections to secure them to the frame and fork, with components that can be trimmed to suit different setups.

Coverage is particularly impressive at the rear, where an extended scoop-shaped section helps keep spray away from the drivetrain as well as the rider. They’re also surprisingly quiet in use, thanks to supplied anti-vibration pads and brush inserts that help keep everything centred, even with tight tyre clearances.

Fitting is more involved than you might expect, though. There are plenty of individual components to position, the adhesive mounting points need careful placement, and the initial installation takes patience. Clearance around the front brake can also be particularly tight with 28mm tyres and calliper brakes, so check your setup before buying. The adhesive fixings can occasionally come loose, too, although spare mounts are supplied.

They’re not the prettiest mudguards, but if your bike isn’t designed for conventional full-length mudguards, the Road Racer Mk3s offer an effective and relatively quiet alternative, with particularly good protection for your drivetrain.

Zefal Shield R35

£40 | Buy here

  • Good rear coverage for clip-on mudguards
  • Extended flap helps protect the rear brake area
  • Affordable, lightweight option for bikes without mudguard mounts 

The Zefal Shield R35 mudguards are a budget-friendly option for road bikes without mudguard eyelets, offering a useful step up in protection from more minimalist clip-on designs. Made from lightweight thermoplastic, they’re secured using rubber mounting blocks and adjustable straps, with an extended rear flap available in three lengths to help catch spray around the rear brake.

Fitting takes a little patience, as getting the mounting blocks and straps correctly positioned can be fiddly, and adjustment is limited once everything is in place. The mounts can also shift slightly on rougher roads, while tight clearance around the front wheel may rule them out for some frames.

Once fitted, the rear guard provides surprisingly good protection for this style of mudguard, although the front offers less coverage and the drivetrain remains exposed. At £40, they’re a practical, removable option for occasional wet-weather riding, provided your frame has sufficient clearance and you don’t mind some setup faff.

Ass Savers Win Wing 2 Road

£24 | Buy here

  • Quick, tool-free fitting with no permanent mounting hardware
  • Lightweight, removable design for bikes without mudguard mounts
  • Adjustable blade lets you fine-tune the positioning to suit your frame 

The Ass Savers Win Wing 2 Road is a minimalist rear mudguard designed to keep the worst of the road spray off your back without the bulk or commitment of full-length mudguards. Weighing just 64g, it attaches to the seatstays using flexible rubber straps, takes only a couple of minutes to fit and is just as easy to remove. The adjustable blade can be positioned to suit your frame, while supplied protection stickers help prevent rubbing against the paintwork.

Despite its small size, it does a surprisingly good job of keeping your back dry, and is impressively quiet over rough roads. However, coverage is limited: the seat tube and drivetrain remain exposed, and the matching Speed Mullet front guard won’t keep your feet completely dry. They’re also not ideal for wet group rides, offering little protection to anyone following behind. A convenient, affordable option for occasional wet-weather riding, but not a substitute for full-length winter mudguards.

How do I choose the right bike mudguards?

Clearance and mounting points

The first thing you need to know is whether or not your bike’s frame has eyelets for attaching full-length mudguards, and if there’s enough clearance between the tyres, frame and fork to accommodate them. Check the manufacturer’s specifications if you’re unsure, and remember that the stated maximum tyre clearance doesn’t necessarily tell you how much room you’ll have left once mudguards are fitted.

If your bike lacks mounting points, clip-on mudguards are an obvious alternative. It’s also possible to fit traditional full-length mudguards using P-clips, which are available from DIY stores. Look for rubber-lined versions to help protect the frame’s finish.

Fortunately, more and more of the best road bikes, particularly endurance bikes, all-road bikes and gravel bikes, now come with mudguard mounts. These aren’t always immediately obvious, as some manufacturers use discreet or hidden eyelets, so it’s worth checking the frame carefully or consulting the bike’s manual.

Length and style

The type and length of mudguard you choose will have a significant impact on how much protection you get. Full-length mudguards offer the most comprehensive coverage, helping to keep spray and road grime off you, your bike and anyone riding behind. They also protect more of the frame and drivetrain, reducing the amount of cleaning and maintenance needed through winter. Don’t overlook the mudflaps, either. These small extensions at the ends of the mudguards can make a noticeable difference to how much spray gets through.

Shorter clip-on fenders are generally lighter, easier to fit and remove, and useful if you only need occasional protection or want to avoid permanent fittings. However, coverage is inevitably more limited. Some designs do a surprisingly good job of keeping spray off your back, but are less effective at protecting your feet, drivetrain or fellow cyclists. Minimalist under-saddle mudguards offer the least protection, primarily shielding your lower back from the worst of the rear-wheel spray.

Brakes and frame compatibility

Traditional full-length mudguards typically attach to the fork crown at the front and the brake bridge at the rear. Check that the necessary mounting points are available, particularly if your bike has disc brakes, as you’ll need a compatible fitting arrangement. Depending on the frame and brake setup, you may also need to work around brake callipers, which can make installation more complicated.

Clip-on designs avoid some of these issues by attaching to the seatstays, fork legs, downtube or seatpost instead. However, they’re not universally compatible either, and mounting straps and rubber blocks need to sit securely against the frame, and limited clearance can make positioning difficult.

If your bike has rim brakes, pay particular attention to the width of the mudguards and the space around the callipers. Mudguards that are too wide can interfere with the brakes or prevent the wheel from turning freely. Even when a manufacturer specifies a maximum tyre width, check the actual clearance on your bike before buying, as tyre dimensions can vary between brands and models.

Fitting and maintenance

It’s also worth considering how much effort you’re prepared to put into installation. Some full-length mudguards require stays to be cut to size, and may need additional spacers or hardware to achieve a secure fit. Others are designed for relatively straightforward installation, while clip-on options can often be fitted without specialist tools or permanent modifications.

Look for adjustable mounting systems if you’re fitting mudguards to an unusual frame shape, but bear in mind that some clip-on designs offer limited scope for repositioning once installed. Frame-protection tape can also be a sensible precaution wherever straps or mounting blocks contact the paintwork. Once fitted, check that all fixings are secure and that the mudguards don’t rub against the tyres, frame or brakes.
